name: Ecuadorian Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Clark 2017 documentation of Ecuadorian Sign Language exists (cited on Glottolog), but as a sign language no word-stress description applies; no stress statement found.

sources.citation: Nasevilla Santillán, Karen Carolina. 2015. Aportes lingüísticos para la sistematización de la lengua de señas de Quito. Disertación de licenciatura, Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador, Quito. 89 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Section 3.4.1 Fonología (pp. 57-61) presents Stokoe's parameters (location, handshape, movement) and minimal pairs for LSQUI; p. 61 says, following Stokoe, that facial expressions and kinesic activity seem to function like the suprasegmental categories of oral languages (intonation, stress, juncture). No statement of where stress falls in a sign; no claim that stress is absent.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page for ecua1243 (Ecuadorian Sign Language)
sources.note: Bibliographic only: one descriptive ref (Nasevilla Santillán 2015, specific_feature), plus Román 2012 dictionary, Mano a Mano 1987 wordlist, Velásquez García 1994 and Santillán 1994 overviews; classification note cites Clark 2017 pp. 17-18 for lexical similarity.

sources.citation: Koulidobrova, Elena, Julio Aguirre, Fernanda Bossano & Jorge Banet. 2026. First steps in the documentation of Ecuadorian Sign Language (LSEC). Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America 11(1). doi:10.3765/plsa.v11i1.6060
sources.note: First community-based documentation report: word order (SVO), agreeing predicates, argument omission, role shift, doubling, ASL contact. Phonology/morpho-phonology named only as ongoing future analysis (1SG articulations, compounding); 'intonation' appears only as an elicitation tag. Nothing on stress.
Classification stub only (lexical similarity per Clark). Nothing on phonology or stress.

sources.citation: Ayala Núñez, Martina Antonella. 2021. Lengua de señas ecuatoriana: diagnóstico de su situación y necesidad de una planificación lingüística. Disertación, Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador, Quito. 98 pp.
sources.note: Sociolinguistic / language-planning study. States (p. ~11 of text) that sign-language phonology (querología) has been the basis of most sign-language research but 'Este no es el caso de la lengua de señas ecuatoriana... no hay estudios lingüísticos propios de la LSEC'. Nothing on stress or prosody.

sources.citation: Clark, Brenda R. 2017. A grammatical sketch of Sivia Sign Language. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Mānoa. 370 pp. (the 'Clark 2017' Glottolog cites for ecua1243, pp. 17-18)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a Harvard login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Phonology and prosody chapters concern Sivia Sign Language (Peru), not LSEC. Ecuador appears only in ch. 2 (pp. 16-18): three governmental dictionaries (SFPL & Mano a Mano 1987; Garcés 2012; CNID 2014), three 'grammatical studies' (Vásquez 2011; Acosta Reyes 2015; Nasevilla Santillán 2015), and 54% lexical similarity between LSP and Ecuadorian SL. No stress statement for LSEC.

sources.citation: Pallo (2025), cited in Koulidobrova et al. 2026 as a morpho-phonological study of 1SG articulations in LSEC (full citation not recovered from the PLSA paper's text layer)
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: The only work identified that analyses LSEC at the (morpho-)phonological level; the same PUCE/CCSU team lists phonology as its next analysis stage, so a future LSEC phonology sketch would come from here.

sources.citation: Acosta Reyes, Viviana Patricia. 2015. El mundo de las personas con dificultades auditivas y su lengua de señas en el Ecuador-provincia de Pichincha: Propuesta de revista sobre el tema. Licenciatura thesis (social communication), Universidad Central del Ecuador, Quito.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Third of Clark's 'grammatical studies'; social-communication thesis, low probability of phonological content, listed for completeness.

sources.citation: Garcés, Lenin Moreno / FENASEC. 2012. Glosario básico de Lengua de Señas Ecuatoriana. Quito: Federación Nacional de Personas Sordas del Ecuador.

sources.note: Source of the body-location and movement/trajectory symbol charts reproduced by Nasevilla 2015 (Ilustraciones 14-15), i.e. it has a phonological-parameter front matter; would show whether any prominence/intensity marking is described.

sources.citation: Román, Gabriel. 2012. Diccionario oficial de lenguaje de señas ecuatorianas. Quito: FENASEC. 678 pp. ISBN 978-9942-9910-1-0 (online successor: CONADIS/CNID 2014 'Diccionario Gabriel Román')
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Only large-scale official description of LSEC; dictionaries of this kind often carry a parametric (querological) introduction. Low probability of a stress statement, but it is the one LSEC reference work not yet inspected.

sources.citation: Vásquez, Paulina A. 2011. Mis manos son mi voz: las personas sordas y la lucha por el reconocimiento de sus derechos lingüísticos en el Ecuador. MA thesis, Universidad Andina Simón Bolívar, Quito.

sources.note: Listed by Clark 2017 among the three 'grammatical studies' of LSEC; title indicates a language-rights study, so a stress statement is unlikely, but it is one of the few LSEC-specific academic works and UASB theses are usually open in its repository.
